# Diencephalon

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > Diencephalon*

[Original Article Link](/library/-60DnS)

---

## Summary

The diencephalon is the <u>caudal</u> part of the forebrain (<u>prosencephalon</u>), located between the <u>midbrain</u> (<u>mesencephalon</u>) and the <u>cerebrum</u> (<u>telencephalon</u>). It consists of the <u>thalamus</u>, <u>hypothalamus</u>, <u>epithalamus</u>, and <u>subthalamus</u>. The <u>thalamus</u> is the relay center for sensory information. The <u>hypothalamus</u> regulates autonomic function and the <u>endocrine system</u>. The <u>epithalamus</u>, which comprises the <u>pineal gland</u>, <u>habenula</u>, <u>habenular commissure</u>, and <u>stria medullaris</u>, regulates the <u>sleep</u>-wake cycle. The <u>subthalamus</u>, which contains the <u>subthalamic nucleus</u>, is part of the indirect <u>basal ganglia</u> circuit and is involved in the inhibition of involuntary movements. The <u>limbic system</u> consists of the <u>amygdala</u>, <u>hypothalamus</u>, <u>anterior</u> <u>thalamus</u>, <u>hippocampus</u>, <u>mammillary bodies</u>, cingulate cortex, and <u>entorhinal cortex</u>. These structures are involved in <u>memory</u> formation, <u>regulation of appetite</u> and satiety, attention, emotional responses, and sexual arousal.

---

## Overview

* Location: <u>caudal</u> portion of the forebrain, situated between the <u>cerebrum</u> and <u>midbrain</u>

* <u>Embryogenesis</u>: arises from <u>prosencephalon</u>

* Composition and function

* <u>Thalamus</u>: relay center of sensory information between subcortical and cortical structures

* <u>Hypothalamus</u>: main center of autonomic function and <u>endocrine system</u> function

* <u>Epithalamus</u>: involved in the regulation of the <u>sleep</u>-wake cycle

* <u>Subthalamus</u>: contains the <u>subthalamic nucleus</u>, a part of the <u>basal ganglia</u>

## Thalamus

### Characteristics




* Location: <u>dorsal</u> part of diencephalon, located above the <u>midbrain</u>

* Function: a group of <u>nuclei</u> constituting the main relay center of ascending sensory information between subcortical and cortical (except for the <u>sense of smell</u>)

* Composition

* Divided into <u>lateral</u>, <u>anterior</u>, <u>medial</u>, and intralaminar nuclear groups and the metathalamic region

* <u>Lateral</u>, <u>anterior</u>, and <u>medial</u> nuclear groups are separated by the Y-shaped internal medullary lamina

* The <u>lateral</u> group can be subdivided into <u>posterior</u>, <u>dorsal</u>, and <u>ventral</u> subgroups





![Anatomical illustration of the thalamus and hypothalamus](media/hqutnrn3o5aple4ccgk9sztc.jpg)

Anatomical illustration of the thalamus and hypothalamus

> [!NOTE]
> <u>Thalamic stroke</u> causes <u>contralateral</u> <u>hemiparesis</u> and hemisensory loss, <u>miotic</u> and unreactive <u>pupils</u>, and <u>upgaze palsy</u> with gaze deviation away from the side of the lesion (a phenomenon known as <u>wrong-way eyes</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Olfaction</u> is the only sensory modality that is not relayed through the <u>thalamus</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> VPL: receives sensory information from the Limbs. VPM: receives sensory information from your Mug (face).




> [!NOTE]
> The Lateral geniculate body processes Light (part of the <u>visual pathway</u>); the Medial geniculate body processes Music (part of the <u>hearing</u> pathway).




### Blood supply [[1]](/library/iRaJ54)




* Mainly derived from branches of the <u>posterior cerebral artery</u> (P1 and <u>P2</u> segments):

* Posterior thalamosubthalamic paramedian arteries

* Area of supply: <u>ventral</u>, intralaminar, and <u>medial</u> nuclear groups

* <u>Infarction</u> symptoms: impaired <u>learning</u>, <u>memory</u> loss, visual disturbance, and <u>confabulation</u>

* Thalamogeniculate arteries

* Area of supply: <u>ventral</u> nuclear group of the <u>thalamus</u>, <u>medial geniculate thalamic nucleus</u>

* <u>Infarction</u> symptoms: impaired movement, <u>contralateral</u> hemisensory loss, <u>thalamic pain syndrome</u>

* Posterior choroidal arteries

* Area of supply: <u>intralaminar nuclei</u>, <u>pulvinar</u>, <u>medial</u>, and <u>lateral geniculate nuclei</u>

* <u>Infarction</u> symptoms: impaired movement, <u>contralateral</u> hemisensory loss, <u>thalamic pain syndrome</u>, <u>visual field</u> loss

* Branches of the <u>posterior communicating artery</u>:
* Anterior thalamosubthalamic paramedian arteries

* Area of supply: <u>anterior</u>, <u>ventral</u>, and intralaminar nuclear groups of the <u>thalamus</u>

* <u>Infarction</u> symptoms: facial asymmetry during emotional displays, <u>memory</u> loss, <u>hemiparesis</u>, <u>apraxia</u>, <u>hemispatial neglect</u>

* For more information on the clinical significance of <u>infarction</u> of the <u>thalamus</u>, see “<u>Thalamic stroke</u>” in “<u>Overview of stroke</u>.”

## Hypothalamus

### Characteristics




* Location: <u>anterior</u> part of the diencephalon, <u>ventral</u> and inferior to the <u>thalamus</u>

* Function

* Control center for the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>

* Regulates hormonal pathways and autonomic functions

* Production of <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>hormones</u> that (e.g., <u>GHRH</u>, <u>somatostatin</u>, <u>dopamine</u>) mostly affect the hormonal secretion of the <u>anterior pituitary gland</u>

* For more information on the function of the <u>hypothalamus</u>, see “<u>Hypothalamus and pituitary gland</u>” in “<u>General endocrinology</u>”

* Composition: four nuclear groups

* Supraoptic (<u>anterior</u>)

* Tuberal (middle)

* Mammillary (<u>posterior</u>)

* Preoptic (<u>anterior</u>-<u>posterior</u>)

* Inputs

* <u>Area postrema</u> in <u>dorsal</u> <u>medulla oblongata</u>

* <u>Vascular organ of lamina terminalis</u>: detects changes in <u>osmolarity</u> with <u>osmoreceptors</u>

> [!NOTE]
> <u>Hypothalamic</u> functions (Thirst and water balance; Adenohypophysis produces <u>releasing hormones</u> that act on the <u>anterior pituitary</u>, Neurohypophysis produces <u>ADH</u> and <u>oxytocin</u> for the <u>posterior pituitary</u>; Hunger; Anger; Temperature; Sexual functions): TAN HATS




> [!NOTE]
> Injury to the Lateral <u>nucleus</u> makes you Lean (due to the absence of hunger), and injury to the VentroMedial <u>nucleus</u> makes you Very Massive (due to the absence of satiety).




> [!NOTE]
> Function of <u>suprachiasmatic nucleus</u> (<u>SCN</u>): Sun Censing Nucleus




> [!NOTE]
> Functions of <u>hypothalamic nuclei</u> (Supraoptic <u>nucleus</u> releases, ADH release, Paraventricular <u>nucleus</u> release, OXytocin): SAD POX




> [!NOTE]
> The MaMmillary bOdY is important for MeMOrY.

### Blood supply




* <u>Anterior</u> <u>hypothalamus</u>: <u>anterior cerebral artery</u> and <u>anterior communicating artery</u>

* Tuberal <u>hypothalamus</u>: <u>posterior communicating artery</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> <u>hypothalamus</u>: <u>posterior communicating artery</u>, <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>, and <u>basilar artery</u>

## Epithalamus and Subthalamus

### Epithalamus




* Location: <u>dorsal</u> diencephalon, superior and <u>posterior</u> to <u>thalamus</u>

* Function

* Connects <u>limbic system</u> to other parts of the <u>brain</u>

* Controls the <u>circadian rhythm</u>

* Composition: <u>habenula</u>, <u>habenular commissure</u>, <u>stria medullaris</u>, and <u>pineal gland</u>

* Blood supply: <u>posterior</u> cerebral <u>artery</u> → <u>posterior choroidal arteries</u>





| Overview of the <u>epithalamus</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Characteristics | Function | Clinical significance |
| Pineal gland | <br><br>* An endocrine gland named after its resemblance to a pine cone<br><br>* Contains specialized <u>neurons</u> (pinealocytes) with endocrine functions<br><br>* Receives input from the <u>suprachiasmatic nucleus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Circadian secretion of <u>melatonin</u> (derived from <u>tryptophan</u>)<br><br>* Regulation of the <u>sleep</u>-wake cycle<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pinealoma</u><br><br>* Calcification  <br><br>* A physiological process that begins in early adulthood<br><br>* <u>Histology</u> and <u>neuroimaging</u> show <u>corpora arenacea</u><br><br><br> |
| Habenula | <br><br>* Connects the <u>pineal gland</u> to the <u>thalamus</u><br><br>* Consists of the <u>habenular nuclei</u><br><br>* Receives input from the <u>stria medullaris</u><br><br>* Projects to cell groups of the <u>tegmentum</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Modulation of:<br><br>* <u>Nociception</u><br><br>* Behavioral response to <u>pain</u> or <u>stress</u><br><br>* <u>Sleep</u>-wake cycle<br><br>* Mood<br><br>* Reproductive behavior<br><br> | <br>* Reduced volume of the <u>habenula</u> has been associated with <u>mood disorders</u> (e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>)<br><br> |
| Habenular commissure | <br>* Fiber bundle that connects the <u>habenular nuclei</u> of both sides<br><br> | <br>* Connection between the <u>habenular nuclei</u><br><br> | <br>* Calcification is common<br><br> |
| Stria medullaris | <br><br>* Fiber bundle that forms a horizontal ridge in the <u>thalamus</u><br><br>* Receives input from the <u>anterior</u> perforated substance, <u>thalamus</u>, and <u>hypothalamus</u><br><br>* Projects to the <u>habenular nuclei</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Connection between the <u>limbic system</u> and <u>habenular nuclei</u><br><br> | <br>* -<br><br> |

### Subthalamus




* Location: <u>lateral</u> to the <u>hypothalamus</u>, <u>rostral</u> to the <u>thalamus</u>, and <u>medial</u> to the <u>internal capsule</u>

* Function: part of the <u>indirect pathway of the basal ganglia</u> circuitry, involved in the modulation <u>motor function</u>

* Composition

* The <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> is the most prominent structure.

* The <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> has excitatory glutamatergic projections to both segments of the <u>globus pallidus</u> and <u>substantia nigra</u>

* Clinical relevance: A lesion of the <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> can lead to <u>contralateral</u> <u>hemiballismus</u>.

* For more information on the <u>subthalamus</u>, see “<u>Basal ganglia</u>” in “<u>The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system</u>.”

---

## Limbic system

### Characteristics




* Function: involved in emotional and behavioral responses, motivation, <u>memory</u>, <u>olfaction</u>, and <u>autonomic nervous system</u> function

* Components

* Areas of the <u>cerebral cortex</u>: hippocampal formation (<u>hippocampus</u>, <u>dentate gyrus</u>, <u>entorhinal cortex</u>), <u>cingulate gyrus</u>

* <u>Nuclei</u>: <u>mammillary bodies</u>, <u>amygdala</u>, <u>anterior thalamic nuclei</u>

* Nerve fiber tracts 

* Cerebral fornix: C-shaped nerve fiber bundle that represents the major output tract of the <u>hippocampus</u>

* Cingulum: nerve fiber bundle connecting <u>cingulate gyrus</u> and <u>entorhinal cortex</u>

* Mammillothalamic tract

* <u>Striae</u> terminalis

| <br>Dentate gyrus  <br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Medial</u> part of the <u>temporal lobe</u><br><br>* <u>Medial</u> to the <u>hippocampus</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Entorhinal cortex</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hippocampus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Memory</u> formation<br><br>* Part of the <u>Papez circuit</u><br><br>* Contains <u>granule cells</u><br><br><br> |
| Entorhinal cortex |  | <br>* <u>Rostral</u> end of the <u>temporal lobe</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Olfactory bulb</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hippocampus</u><br><br>* <u>Dentate gyrus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Memory</u> formation<br><br>* Part of the <u>Papez circuit</u><br><br>* Olfactory <u>associative learning</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Mammillary bodies  <br> |  | <br><br>* Part of the <u>hypothalamus</u><br><br>* On the <u>distal</u> <u>anterior</u> end of the <u>cerebral fornix</u> bilaterally<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Amygdala</u><br><br>* <u>Hippocampus</u><br><br>* Fornix<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Anterior thalamic nuclei</u> (via mammillothalamic tract)<br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the <u>Papez circuit</u><br><br>* <u>Memory</u> formation<br><br><br> |
| Amygdala |  | <br><br>* Deep in the <u>medial</u> part of the <u>temporal lobe</u> (<u>uncus</u>)<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> to the <u>hippocampus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hypothalamus</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebral cortex</u><br><br>* Olfactory cortex<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hypothalamus</u> (via <u>striae</u> terminalis)<br><br> | <br><br>* Relays emotional reactions, especially to fear, aggression, and <u>anxiety</u><br><br>* Involved in decision-making<br><br>* Regulates the activity of the autonomic nervous and endocrine systems<br><br>* Recognition of emotional facial expressions<br><br><br> |
| Cingulate gyrus |  | <br><br>* Superior to the corpus callosum bilaterally<br><br>* On the <u>medial</u> surface of the frontal and <u>parietal lobe</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Anterior thalamic nuclei</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hippocampus</u><br><br>* <u>Entorhinal cortex</u> (via <u>cingulum</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* Part of the <u>Papez circuit</u><br><br> |
| <u>Anterior thalamic nuclei</u> |  | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> part of the <u>thalamus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mammillary bodies</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebral fornix</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cingulate gyrus</u><br><br>* <u>Entorhinal cortex</u><br><br>* <u>Cingulum</u><br><br><br> |  |

### Papez circuit




* Description

* An anatomical circuit within the <u>limbic system</u> that starts and ends in the <u>hippocampus</u>

* Involved in the formation and storage of memories and the control of emotions (e.g., sexual desire, pleasure, fear, and <u>anxiety</u>)

* Commonly affected in <u>Alzheimer disease</u> and <u>Korsakoff syndrome</u>

* Circuit: <u>pyramidal cells</u> of the <u>hippocampus</u> → fornix → <u>mammillary bodies</u> (<u>hypothalamus</u>) → mammillothalamic tract → <u>anterior</u> thalamic <u>nucleus</u> → <u>anterior</u> limb of the internal capsule → cingulate <u>gyrus</u> → <u>cingulum</u> → entorhinal cortex → <u>hippocampus</u>  

* The <u>hippocampus</u> receives input from cortical associations such as the <u>cingulum</u>, <u>cingulate gyrus</u>, and parahippocampal <u>gyrus</u>.

* The <u>hippocampus</u> receives input from and sends output to the <u>amygdala</u>.

* The <u>amygdala</u> is involved in <u>emotional regulation</u> and encoding of emotionally influenced <u>memory</u> (positive or negative).





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>limbic system</u> is responsible for the famous 5 F's: Feeding, Fleeing, Fighting, Feeling, and … Sex.

## Clinical significance

* <u>Major neurocognitive disorders</u>: <u>Alzheimer disease</u>

* <u>Cerebrovascular diseases</u>

* <u>Overview of stroke</u>

* <u>Cerebral venous thrombosis</u>

* <u>Vascular dementia</u>

* <u>Epidural hematoma</u>

* <u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Subdural hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Intracerebral hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Brain tumors</u>

* <u>Pinealoma</u>

* <u>Astrocytoma</u>

* <u>Meningioma</u>

* Genetic disorders

* <u>Tay-Sachs disease</u>

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Phenylketonuria</u>

* <u>Niemann-Pick disease</u>

* <u>Seizure disorders</u>: <u>focal seizures and syndromes</u>

* Other neurological disorders

* <u>Hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Neurocutaneous syndromes</u>

* <u>Horner syndrome</u>

* <u>Tourette syndrome</u>

* <u>Cerebral palsy</u>

* <u>Dystonia</u>

* <u>Spinocerebellar ataxia</u>

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u>

* <u>Wallenberg syndrome</u>

* <u>Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome</u>

* <u>Anterograde amnesia</u>

* <u>Hypothalamic</u> dysfunctions

* Neurogenic hyperthermia: a noninfectious cause of <u>fever</u>, due to dysfunction of the <u>anterior</u> <u>hypothalamus</u> (usually after <u>head trauma</u>) that impairs the body's ability to dissipate heat

* <u>Hypothermia</u>

* <u>Insomnia</u>

* <u>Diabetes insipidus</u>

* <u>Kallmann syndrome</u>

* <u>Hyperphagia</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Anorexia nervosa</u>

* <u>Failure to thrive</u>

* <u>Starvation</u>
